_note: Sample utterances shown as a live cue card during Foundations sessions only. Beginners can read these aloud. Plain, high-frequency clinical English.

categories.name: 1) Greeting & introducing yourself
phrases: Hello, my name is ___. I'm a medical student.
Nice to meet you. May I check your name, please?
How would you like me to call you?
Is it okay if I ask you some questions about how you're feeling?

categories.name: 2) Opening — let the patient talk
phrases: What brings you in today?
How can I help you today?
Tell me more about that.
Please go on, I'm listening.

categories.name: 3) Asking about the symptom (plain SOCRATES)
phrases: When did it start?
Where exactly do you feel it?
Can you describe what it feels like?
On a scale of one to ten, how bad is it?
Does anything make it better or worse?
Has it changed since it started?

categories.name: 4) Following up & checking
phrases: Could you say a little more about that?
Just to make sure I understand, you mean ___?
Has anything like this happened before?
Is there anything else that's been bothering you?

categories.name: 5) Showing empathy
phrases: That sounds really difficult.
I can see this is worrying you.
Thank you for telling me that.
It's understandable to feel that way.
Take your time, there's no rush.

categories.name: 6) Checking understanding & explaining simply
phrases: Let me make sure I've understood you correctly.
Would it help if I explained that in a simpler way?
Does that make sense so far?
Please stop me if anything is unclear.

categories.name: 7) Closing the conversation
phrases: Is there anything you'd like to ask me?
Do you have any concerns we haven't talked about?
Thank you for your time today.
I'd like to summarize what we've discussed.

categories.name: 8) US clinic signposting & permission
phrases: Before I ask more questions, is it okay if we talk about your symptoms?
I may need to ask some personal questions. You can skip anything you are not comfortable with.
I'll summarize what I heard, then we can talk about next steps.
I want to make sure I explain this clearly.

categories.name: 9) Clarifying patient language
phrases: When you say ___, what does that mean for you?
Could you show me where you feel it?
I didn't quite catch that. Could you say it one more time?
Just to check, do you mean the pain comes and goes?

categories.name: 10) Plain-language rewrites
phrases: High blood pressure means the force of blood in your blood vessels is higher than we want.
A side effect is an unwanted effect a medicine can cause.
Fasting means not eating or drinking for a set time before the test.
Benign means it is not cancer.

categories.name: 11) Read-back and team communication
phrases: Let me read that back to make sure I got it right.
I'm calling about ___, a ___-year-old patient with ___.
My main concern is ___.
Could you please advise on the next step?

categories.name: 12) IMG interview storytelling
phrases: One experience that shaped me was ___.
What I learned from that was ___.
I adapted by ___.
In a US clinical team, I would clarify expectations early.

categories.name: 13) Register switching: patient to team
phrases: For the patient, I would say: in simple terms, ___.
For the team, I would say: the main issue is ___.
For the attending, I would say: my assessment is ___.
The same idea in plain English is ___.

categories.name: 14) Fast listening and read-back
phrases: Let me read that back to make sure I got it right.
I heard room ___, medication ___, dose ___, and time ___.
Could you repeat the number after ___?
Did you say before rounds or after rounds?

categories.name: 15) Repair phrases when you miss fast English
phrases: Sorry, I missed the last part.
Could you say that one more time a little more slowly?
I caught the first part, but not the medication name.
Could you spell the patient's last name?

categories.name: 16) US team communication
phrases: Quick update: the patient is ___.
The pending item is ___.
My main concern right now is ___.
Could you help me follow up on ___?

categories.name: 17) Concise attending updates
phrases: My one-liner is: ___.
My assessment is ___.
I am concerned about ___ because ___.
The next step I would recommend is ___.

categories.name: 18) Follow-up — opening & linking to the last visit
phrases: How have you been since your last visit?
How have you been since we started the ___?
Last time we talked about ___. How has that been going?
Today I'd like to check in on how things have been.

categories.name: 19) Follow-up — checking if the plan is working
phrases: How has the medicine/treatment been working for you?
What have your readings/symptoms looked like since your last visit?
Has it gotten better, worse, or stayed about the same?
Tell me more about how that's been.

categories.name: 20) Follow-up — asking about adherence (nonjudgmental)
phrases: How has it been taking the medicine every day?
A lot of people find it hard to remember every dose — how about you?
Have you missed or skipped any doses?
There's no wrong answer here — I just want to understand how it's been.

categories.name: 21) Follow-up — side effects & safety check
phrases: Have you noticed any side effects since starting this?
Have you had any new or worsening symptoms?
Is there anything that's been bothering you that we haven't talked about?
Have you had any warning signs, like chest pain or shortness of breath?

categories.name: 22) Follow-up — explaining results & next steps in plain English
phrases: Your results show ___, which means ___.
That's a good sign / that's something we should watch.
Based on how you're doing, I'd suggest we ___.
Let's agree on what to do next and when you should come back.

categories.name: 23) Follow-up — closing with a safety net
phrases: Is there anything about the plan you'd like to ask me?
Could you tell me in your own words what the plan is?
Come back sooner if ___.
Call us right away if you notice ___.
